title: Fourier series

source.author: 20watts
source.notes: Run live by src/sims/fourier.ts: seven circles turning at odd multiples of one speed, their radii shrinking as 1/n, the tip drawing a square wave. The program is the museum's own, CC0.

object.description:
Any repeating shape, Fourier claimed, is a sum of pure sine waves. He needed it to solve how heat spreads through a solid, and his 1822 Théorie analytique de la chaleur made the claim stick, though it took a century of analysis to say exactly when it is true. The panel shows it as circles riding on circles: the first turns once a cycle, the next three times as fast at a third the size, the next five times at a fifth, and so on. The same idea takes music apart into its overtones, images into frequencies, and is what every signal, from a phone call to a JPEG, passes through.

The circles here are turning as you watch, not replaying: the tip of the last one traces, as it goes, a square wave, the corners sharpening with every circle added.
facts: Seven terms are drawn here; a perfect square wave would need infinitely many.
Ptolemy used circles on circles to predict planets; Fourier's are the same geometry, pointed at a different question.
Fourier was also the first, in 1824, to describe what is now called the greenhouse effect.
The fast Fourier transform of 1965 made the sum cheap enough to compute everywhere.

tour: Fourier's claim of 1822: any repeating shape is a sum of pure waves. Circles riding on circles trace a square wave; every circle added sharpens the corners.
